introduction-when-autoscaling-is-too-slo.core: Autoscaling takes minutes; traffic spikes take seconds. When demand exceeds capacity, a service that tries to serve everything slows down for everyone and can collapse into a metastable state. Load shedding deliberately rejects some requests quickly so the rest succeed, keeping goodput high until capacity catches up.

first_principles.problem: A flash sale triples traffic in 30 seconds, autoscaling needs 5 minutes, and the site goes down completely.

analogy.title: A nightclub at capacity
analogy.story: The bouncer turns some people away so those inside stay safe, rather than letting everyone crush in.
analogy.breaks: Clubs have fixed capacity; services can scale up after a delay.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Partial service instead of total outage.

check.q: Why is load shedding needed even with autoscaling?
check.a: Autoscaling reacts in minutes, while spikes overwhelm capacity in seconds.

goodput-vs-throughput.core: Throughput counts all requests processed; goodput counts requests completed successfully within their deadline (useful work). Under overload, throughput can stay high while goodput collapses, because servers spend effort on requests that time out before responses arrive. Shedding and deadline awareness preserve goodput.

first_principles.problem: Dashboards show the service handling 10,000 rps during an incident, yet users see 90% failures.

analogy.title: A pizza shop delivering cold pizzas
analogy.story: It's busy making pizzas, but customers who've given up won't pay.
analogy.breaks: Cold pizzas are visible; wasted server work looks like normal activity.

example.title: Throughput vs goodput
flow: Load 1.5× without shedding: throughput flat, goodput → 20%

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shedding keeps useful work at maximum.

check.q: Why can throughput stay high while goodput collapses?
check.a: Servers keep processing requests whose clients have already timed out, so the work is wasted.

priority-queues-who-gets-saved.core: When shedding, not all requests are equal: checkout matters more than recommendations, user-facing more than batch, retries less than first attempts. Assign criticality (e.g. Google's CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE) propagated across calls, and shed lowest priority first so the most valuable work survives.

first_principles.problem: During overload, shedding randomly drops checkout requests while background analytics continue.
truths: Priority must flow through call chains.
Some traffic can safely wait or fail.

analogy.title: A hospital emergency department triage
analogy.story: The most urgent patients are seen first; minor cases wait or are redirected.
analogy.breaks: Triage nurses assess each patient; systems rely on labels set by callers.

check.a: They're additional load caused by the overload, and first attempts usually have more value.

admission-control-the-bouncer.core: Admission control decides at the door whether to accept a request, based on current load: concurrency limits (adaptive algorithms like Netflix's concurrency-limits or TCP-Vegas/AIMD-style), queue time, CPU or token buckets. Rejecting at admission is cheap and keeps in-flight work within capacity, protecting latency for admitted requests.

first_principles.problem: A static rate limit is either too high (overload on slow days) or too low (rejects traffic on good days).
truths: Capacity varies with request mix and dependencies.
derivation: Reject when **limit reached** or **queue time too high**.

analogy.title: A bouncer who watches how crowded the room feels
analogy.story: Instead of a fixed headcount, they let people in while the room still feels comfortable.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers judge intuitively; algorithms need tuning to avoid oscillation.

check.q: What advantage does an adaptive concurrency limit have over a fixed rate limit?
check.a: It adjusts to the service's real, changing capacity based on observed latency.
